paper_title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates proposals under deliberately limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to retain promising candidates for costly empirical evaluation. We evaluate BVSR across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks. Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness, and produces a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than existing state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines. Learning from prior proposal outcomes on the task further improves candidate selection, discarding half of the candidates while retaining most top-performing proposals. When incorporated into existing AI-scientist workflows, BVSR achieves stronger discoveries across gene expression analysis, drug response prediction, anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction. These results suggest that effective AI scientists should use information differently across stages of discovery: constrain task-specific information during exploration while exploiting accumulated empirical experience on the task.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: As large language models (LLMs) have made substantial gains in reasoning and long-horizon task execution, growing body of work explores deploying AI agents for scientific discovery [11, 24]. Existing studies demonstrate that AI agents can outperform the best human-designed solutions across wide range of tasks, including mathematical proof [14], mathematical discovery [33], optimization [29], and subset of scientific problems [57]. However, strong performance alone does not establish the creativity of the proposed methods. Prior work has identified limitations in the novelty of AI-generated proposals, including tendency to explore incremental modifications or extensions of existing approaches [15, 54]. key challenge is therefore to develop AI agents that can reliably generate proposals that are creative. Addressing this challenge requires both assessing creativity rigorously and developing methods to improve it. Since the 1950s, psychologists have systematically studied how creativity should be judged in humans [34, 44]. Their work identifies three defining properties of creative ideas: novelty, effectiveness, and non-obviousness [39]. These properties distinguish creativity from performance alone: an idea must work, but its originality and whether its success could have been anticipated also matter. This perspective is captured by quantitative definition [40]: Creativity = Originality Utility Non-obviousness = (1 p) (1 v), (1) where is the probability of generating an idea, is its tested utility, and represents prior knowledge of its effectiveness. Originality captures whether an idea is uncommon rather than something that many others would propose. Utility reflects whether the idea actually works in practice. Non-obviousness concerns whether its effectiveness is known in advance. In this paper, we adopt this definition to assess the creativity of AI-generated proposals. To improve the creativity of AI agents, prior work has relied mainly on prompt engineering, retrieval augmentation, and variety of search methods: instructing the agent to be novel [37], supplying it with literature as inspiration [50], or iteratively refining and selecting among many candidates according to search heuristics [20]. Each of these approaches, however, has serious limitations. Prompt engineering yields diminishing returns on frontier models [49]. Literature is valuable reference, but the literature an agent retrieves for itself suffers from the same lack of diversity as its own proposals [13, 38]. Heuristic search methods rely on fine-grained signal, whereas most scientific problems offer at best coarse metric of how well finished proposal works [52]. Motivated by these limitations, we draw on the theory of Blind Variation (BV) and Selective Retention (SR) to guide how AI agents generate and select proposals [5]. This theory describes creative discovery as process involving two complementary stages. The first is blind variation: scientists generate diverse ideas without foreknowledge of which will succeed, sometimes drawing inspiration from experiences unrelated to the immediate problem [9, 42]. The second is selective retention: based on prior experience, they discard ideas that are clearly unreasonable and retain plausible ones for further investigation. Similarly, we find that in AI agents, providing too much task information during proposal generation causes the model to anchor on familiar approaches. As illustrated in Figure 1, our method on blind variation first limits the task information available during generation. We then use selective retention to learn, as scientist does by working on problem, from proposals already verified on that task and their empirical outcomes to identify promising candidates for further evaluation. We first show that limiting task information during proposal generation can improve creativity. We provide an intuition for its effect on originality under information-induced anchoring, and validate its benefits empirically across five models and 12 scientific tasks. Across these settings, BV outperforms state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines in originality and non-obviousness, while generating larger share of highly creative and useful proposals. We then develop SR to 2 learn from previously verified proposals and their empirical outcomes, using pairwise objective that separates high-utility proposals from the rest. SR retains top proposals more effectively than prompting-based methods, in-context learning, and supervised fine-tuning. Finally, we integrate BVSR into SimpleTES [56], an existing common adopted AI scientist workflow, where it largely improves discovery performance over the original baselines.

sections.title: 3 Blind Variation: Limited Information Induces More Creativity
sections.content: In this section, we show that providing model with too much task information during proposal generation steers it toward common, less novel approaches. This substantially reduces the originality and non-obviousness of its proposals and, in turn, limits the utility of its top proposals. As illustrated in Figure 1(a), blind variation limits task information during idea generation to encourage exploration beyond familiar approaches.

sections.title: 3.2 Experimental Setup
sections.content: To test this empirically, we use Claude Opus 5 to summarize the full problem statement S, producing contexts with varying amounts of information for the same task. Appendix shows example contexts. We then evaluate proposal creativity under each context. Further details on the models, benchmarks, and settings are provided in Appendix B. For each task, each model, and each information level, we generate 112 proposals. Benchmarks. We evaluate 12 tasks across four scientific domains. (1) Biology. We use four single-cell analysis tasks [25], namely cell-cell communication, label projection, perturbation prediction, and spatially variable genes. (2) Astrodynamics. We use the Cassini [30] and Voyager 2 [18] trajectory design problems. (3) Machine Learning. We use unsupervised anomaly detection and post-hoc probability calibration from MLS Bench [27], along with scaling-law discovery in pretraining and U-shaped / double-descent regime from SLDBench [22]. (4) Neuroscience. We use neural activity forecasting from ZAPBench [26] with prediction horizons of 16 and 32. Models. We evaluate five mainstream LLMs to assess whether our findings generalize across model families. These include DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro [6], GLM-5.3 Flash, GLM-5.2 [10], and Kimi-K3 [48]. All models have reasoning enabled and access to OpenAlex [31] for literature search.

sections.content: Figure 2 shows how creativity, utility, originality, and non-obviousness change as the amount of task information increases. Each dot represents the proposals generated by one model for one benchmark at one information level. Since AI scientist tasks place particular value on highly creative and highly useful methods, we first examine how top creativity and top utility vary with information level. The trend line follows the 95th percentile (a, b) or the mean (c, d) of the dots. Percentages give its change from 0 to 140 bits. As information increases, the relative frequency of proposals ranked in the benchmarks top 1% for creativity or utility generally decreases, while mean originality and mean non-obviousness decline substantially. ranked in the top 1% within each benchmark, according to creativity and utility, respectively. The vertical position of each dot indicates relative frequency, computed as the fraction of its proposals that fall into this top 1%, divided by 1%. We find that models generally produce larger share of these top-ranked proposals at lower information levels. We next examine whether originality and non-obviousness follow similar pattern. We plot mean originality and mean non-obviousness against information level and find that both decline substantially as the amount of task information increases. Across proposals generated by five models on 12 tasks, these results provide systematic evidence that increasing task information reduces the relative frequency of highly creative proposals, supporting the conclusion that limited information can induce greater creativity. We call this approach of improving model creativity by limiting the information provided Blind Variation (BV).

sections.title: 4 Selective Retention: Learning from Scientific Experience
sections.content: Blind variation deliberately reduces task-specific guidance during idea generation, but scientific discovery should not ignore what is learned by working on the task. Just as scientists develop judgment about problem by testing ideas on it, we formulate selective retention as learning from experience on the task itself. Each proposal previously verified on the task provides pair consisting of candidate and its empirical outcome. From these proposaloutcome pairs, we learn scoring function that decides which new candidates for that task should be retained for expensive execution. As illustrated in Figure 1(b), selective retention (SR) uses this learned judgment to reduce the number of candidates requiring empirical verification while preserving promising proposals.

sections.title: 4.1 Motivation
sections.content: Verification can be time-consuming in many scientific tasks: wet-lab experiments may take months, and machine learning experiments may require substantial GPU computation [43]. natural approach is to prompt an LLM to inspect candidates. However, as our comparison below shows, these prompting-based approaches offer limited preservation of top candidates. This motivates learning screener rather than relying exclusively on prompted judgments. The learning objective must also reflect the purpose of screening. Aggregating many such comparisons trains the selector to exploit past outcomes when screening its future candidates. Experimental Setup. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we use 5,783 proposals generated by the five proposer models on the 12 tasks in Section 3. Our training dataset consists of separate set of 40,733 proposals on the same tasks. Implementation details are provided in Appendix B.4. To assess whether the model can identify low-quality proposals, we ask it to rank the candidates and discard those ranked lowest. We vary the discard ratio and measure the fraction of top candidates kept. Higher curves indicate better preservation. All screeners receive the same task specification and candidate implementation. We compare SR with four zero-shot prompting-based judges: Pointwise judge assigns absolute scores, Setwise judge repeatedly identifies weak candidates in groups, Listwise judge aggregates sliding-window rankings in the style of RankGPT [45], and Tournament judge uses six rounds of Swiss-system pairwise comparisons [38]. The in-context learning (ICL) judge also sees four similar verified proposals and their outcomes from the SR training set. We also compare with SFT using the same backbone, trained with mean-squared error. Findings. Figure 3 shows that learned SR preserves top candidates much more effectively than prompting-based screeners. The in-context learning baseline, despite seeing verified outcomes of similar proposals, performs no significantly better than zero-shot judges. SFT improves preservation over many prompt-based methods. Nevertheless, it remains less effective than SR. This result is consistent with the motivation that accurate prediction throughout the distribution is different objective from keeping exceptional candidates out of the discard set. At discard ratio of 50%, SR preserves 79% of the top-5% proposals by creativity and 82% of the top-5% proposals by utility. We therefore use this SR model to discard the lowest-ranked 50% of proposals in later experiments.

sections.title: 5.1 Cross-field Discovery
sections.content: Beyond the gains of BV and SR individually, we evaluate whether combining information-limited generation with experience-based selection improves end-to-end scientific discovery. We evaluate its effectiveness by integrating it into SimpleTES [56]. We compare SimpleTES with and without BVSR on five tasks introduced earlier: gene expression analysis (spatially variable genes), drug response prediction (perturbation prediction), anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction (ZAPBench horizon 16). We use Kimi-K3 for both configurations. Following the SimpleTES setup, we run four parallel search trajectories, each generating 40 proposals per iteration, and run for 10 iterations. Figure 4 plots the best score against the cumulative number of empirically verified proposals. BVSR achieves higher final scores on all five tasks and exceeds the original workflows final score with fewer verification steps. These results show that BVSR can improve discovery performance when incorporated into existing AI scientist workflows. Figure 4. Integrating BVSR into SimpleTES. Best task score as function of verification steps on five scientific tasks. BVSR improves final score and reaches strong solutions with fewer steps. Numbers give how many times fewer verified proposals SimpleTES + BVSR needs to reach SimpleTESs final score (dotted line).

sections.title: 5.2 Case Study
sections.content: We describe three example best programs found by BVSR in Table 2. Each surpasses the best program found by SimpleTES under the same budget and the strongest existing baselines on their tasks. Table 2. Best programs of our methods and of SimpleTES on example tasks (higher is better). Best baseline: SPARK-X for gene expression analysis, Isolation Forest for anomaly detection. Task Ours SimpleTES Best Baseline Gene Expression Analysis Anomaly Detection Scaling Law Discovery 0.918 0.679 0.967 0.906 0.629 0.940 0.853 [60] 0.491 [23] N/A Spatially variable genes via the nudged elastic band. The task is to rank genes by how strongly their expression is organized in space on tissue section. The program borrows the nudged elastic band method from transition-state theory [17], which finds minimum-energy path by relaxing chain of images under two projected forces: the true force perpendicular to the path and spring force along it. It takes the heat-flow trajectory of each genes expression field on the tissue graph, from the observed field to the uniform one, and computes at every image the component of robust energy gradient perpendicular to the path. For pure noise, the heat-flow path is already the minimum-energy path, and this component vanishes; spatial patterns bend the path, so the perpendicular force grows with pattern strength and becomes the genes score. It reaches 0.918, against 0.906 for SimpleTES and 0.853 for SPARK-X, the best method on OpenProblems. Anomaly detection via finite-momentum pairing. The task asks for an anomaly detector with at most 10,000 parameters, scored on four tabular datasets. The program transplants the nonuniform (FFLO) superconducting state [21], in which two species with mismatched Fermi surfaces still pair by giving each pair nonzero momentum, so that the order parameter oscillates in space. Its two species are two scores that often disagree: marginal tail evidence from empirical distribution functions, and geometric evidence from robust covariance and Gaussian mixture of the normal mass. Instead of averaging them, it pairs them with an oscillating modulation along the direction in which they disagree most, relaxes the recovered pairing signal on nearest-neighbour graph and adds it to the combined score. With no trained network it reaches 0.679, against 0.629 for SimpleTES and 0.491 for Isolation Forest. Scaling law via assignment-game prices. The task is to find formula with at most 26 parameters for the final training loss as function of learning rate, batch size, data size and model size. The program draws on the assignment game of Shapley and Shubik [36], whose optimal matching is linear program with competitive prices as dual variables. It solves one fixed, entropy-regularized assignment problem between two grids in the (log learning rate, log batch size) plane and uses the resulting price field as fixed surface that reshapes the loss basin near the optimal learning rate and batch size. The law adds power laws in data and model size and convex bowl around scale-dependent optimum, and fits only two parameters. It reaches 0.967 held-out R2.

sections.title: 5.3 Ablation Study
sections.content: To assess the individual contributions of BV and SR, we compare four configurations: the original SimpleTES, SimpleTES with BV alone, SimpleTES with SR alone, and the full BVSR. We evaluate all four configurations on gene expression analysis and scaling law discovery, and track the best task score against verification steps. Figure 5 shows that BV and SR each improve the final score over SimpleTES, and that combining them works best on both tasks. On gene expression analysis, BV mainly raises the final score and SR mainly speeds up discovery, while BVSR achieves larger gain than either. On scaling law discovery, BVSR again reaches higher score earlier than BV or SR. Because BVSR improves upon the stronger component on each task, the two components are complementary.

sections.title: 5.4 Human Validation
sections.content: Figure 5. Ablation study. Best task score versus verification steps for four SimpleTES configurations. Higher is better. We conduct two human studies to validate the LLM judgments underlying originality and nonobviousness. The former relies on grouping semantically equivalent proposals to estimate their frequencies, while the latter assesses whether prior knowledge suggests that proposal will work. Detailed protocols are provided in Appendix F. Originality. Five PhD-level researchers each annotate 30 proposal pairs, yielding 150 pairs in total. The sample is balanced between pairs grouped together and pairs assigned to different groups 9 by the LLM, and covers multiple tasks, proposer models, and generation methods. Evaluators judge whether the proposals express the same underlying mechanism. 84% of pairs grouped together by the LLM are also judged equivalent by humans (95% CI [0.74, 0.92]), while 73% of pairs assigned to different groups are judged distinct (95% CI [0.61, 0.82]). These results support the semantic-equivalence judgments used to estimate originality. Non-obviousness. Five PhD-level researchers evaluate 150 high-quality proposals from BV and Analogical Reasoning (AR) under blinded conditions. All sampled proposals achieve verified scores above the best baseline for their respective tasks. Evaluators see the task name and summaries of the source paper and proposed method. The summaries are rewritten in uniform style, and method identifiers are removed. Evaluators assess how readily proposals effectiveness could be inferred from the paper and their own knowledge of the literature, using 15 scale with higher scores indicating greater non-obviousness. Human ratings correlate with the automatic non-obviousness score 1 ˆv at = 0.56 (95% CI [0.45, 0.67]). BV proposals receive mean rating of 3.64, compared with 2.97 for AR, difference of 0.67 points (95% CI [0.33, 0.99], = 0.0006). These results support the automatic non-obviousness score and show that BVs advantage persists under expert judgment.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: AI Scientists. Recent work increasingly connects language models to scientific workflows. Coscientist integrates research planning with laboratory automation, while Agent Laboratory and Virtual Lab organize research through specialized agents and human guidance [2, 35, 46]. The AI Scientist extends automation across ideation, experimentation, and manuscript preparation [24]. AlphaEvolve and SimpleTES organize proposal generation and execution [29, 56]. These systems provide capable discovery workflows, but their effectiveness also depends on the candidates they explore. Our work studies how task information shapes proposal generation and how empirical outcomes from previous proposals can guide which new candidates are selected for verification. 10 Creativity in Humans. Associative theories explain creativity through connections between previously remote concepts [8, 28]. Studies show that familiar categories and example solutions can constrain subsequent ideas [16, 51]. Research on incubation further suggests that temporarily setting problem aside can improve creative problem solving [41]. Idea selection presents separate challenge: people often favor feasible and desirable candidates at the expense of originality [32]. Together with Campbells blind-variation-and-selective-retention theory [5], these findings help explain the relationship between information and creativity. We investigate whether reducing task information during ideation can encourage exploration in AI scientists. Creativity in AI. Computational creativity distinguishes combinational, exploratory, and transformational processes [1]. Recent work evaluates LLM creativity through divergent-thinking tasks and the diversity of repeated generations [19, 59]. Beyond text generation, Creative Agents incorporates imagination into embodied planning for open-ended construction tasks [4]. Methods for diversifying outputs include verbalized sampling [58], which elicits distributions over responses, and analogical reasoning [37], which transfers relational structures across scientific domains. Our approach adds task information level as distinct control for creative generation.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied how information should be used at different stages of automated scientific discovery. Our results suggest that more information is not uniformly beneficial. During idea generation, detailed task information can anchor language models toward familiar mechanisms and reduce the probability of generating creative proposals. Blind Variation mitigates this effect by limiting task information. After generation, empirical experience earned on the task can guide which new candidates deserve expensive verification. Selective Retention learns this decision from proposaloutcome data. Together, these findings suggest broader design principle for AI scientists: separate the information used for exploration from the experience used for selection.

sections.title: F Human Validation Protocols
sections.content: This section details the human evaluation protocols used in Section 5.4. F.1 Originality Our originality measure depends on grouping proposals that express the same underlying scientific or algorithmic idea. To validate this semantic-equivalence step, we construct set of 150 proposal pairs, balanced between pairs grouped together and pairs assigned to different groups by the LLM evaluator. The pairs are sampled across tasks, proposer models, and generation methods. Five PhD-level researchers each evaluate 30 pairs. For each pair, the evaluator judges whether the two proposals express essentially the same underlying mechanism, ignoring differences in wording and implementation details. Pairs marked Unsure (4 in total) are excluded from the agreement analysis. An example evaluation sheet is provided in Appendix G.1. F.2 Non-obviousness We sample 150 high-quality proposals from BV and AR, defined as proposals whose verified score exceeds the best baseline of their task. We remove all method identifiers and ask five PhD-level researchers to evaluate their non-obviousness. For each proposal, evaluators are shown the task name, summary of the source paper, and summary of the proposed method. Both summaries are rewritten by Claude Opus 5 into uniform style to reduce cues that could reveal the generating method. Evaluators rate non-obviousness on 15 scale, considering how readily the methods effectiveness on the task could be inferred from the source paper and their own knowledge of the literature. Higher scores indicate greater non-obviousness. Proposals are split into forms of 30, each balanced across tasks and methods and presented in random order. Each evaluator completes one form. An example evaluation sheet is provided in Appendix G.2.
